traps.name: Prompt for a guarantee
traps.description: Uses a system-prompt instruction or few-shot examples when the behavior must be guaranteed (ordering, compliance, money, safety).
traps.principle: A prompt is a probabilistic nudge. Use hooks, prerequisite gates, schemas or tool contracts when compliance must be guaranteed.
examples: Adding "always verify the customer before refunding" to the system prompt when refunds must never run without a verified ID.
Telling the model "never refund more than $500" instead of blocking larger refunds in a hook.

traps.name: Over-engineering
traps.description: Adds a classifier, routing layer, extra agent or merge when a small direct fix works.
traps.principle: Fix the root cause with the smallest change that works. Better descriptions come before new layers.
examples: Training a routing classifier because two tools with vague descriptions get mixed up.
Adding a supervisor agent to check a single tool call that a prerequisite gate could enforce.

traps.name: Treating the symptom
traps.description: Renames, shortens, retries or reassigns without fixing why it fails.
traps.principle: Find the cause (overlap, missing info, a permanent error) and fix that.
examples: Retrying an extraction three more times when the field is simply absent from the document.
Shortening a tool name when the real problem is that its description overlaps with another tool's.

traps.name: Wrong configuration layer
traps.description: Puts shared config in user or `.local` files, personal config in committed files, or enforcement in CLAUDE.md.
traps.principle: Team config goes in committed project files, personal config in `~/.claude` or `.local`. CLAUDE.md is guidance, not enforcement.
examples: Putting team coding standards in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, so new teammates never get them.
Committing a personal experimental MCP server to the project `.mcp.json`.

traps.name: Throwing away state
traps.description: Clears history, restarts or errors out when the state could be kept.
traps.principle: Compact into a case-facts or state block and keep going. Resume rather than restart.
examples: Clearing the conversation when context runs low, losing the order numbers the customer already gave.
Starting a new investigation session from scratch when `--resume` would keep the earlier analysis.

traps.name: Misreading a parameter
traps.description: Treats a parameter as doing something it doesn't (`max_tokens` as the input window, temperature for "nuance", strict mode as semantic validation).
traps.principle: Know what each parameter controls. Output length is not the context window, and schema validity is not correctness.
examples: Raising `max_tokens` to fit a longer document into the context.
Assuming strict JSON schema mode will catch line items that don't add up to the stated total.

traps.name: Going around the coordinator
traps.description: Subagents talk to each other or write to shared context or storage directly.
traps.principle: Hub-and-spoke: all communication, routing and error handling go through the coordinator.
examples: Letting the search subagent send its results straight to the synthesis subagent.
Having subagents write findings to a shared database that others read without the coordinator.

traps.name: Unreliable proxy
traps.description: Decides on sentiment, all caps, self-reported confidence or response length.
traps.principle: Decide on explicit, verifiable criteria. Sentiment is not complexity, and model self-confidence is poorly calibrated.
examples: Escalating whenever sentiment analysis scores the customer as angry.
Skipping human review for any extraction where the model says it is 95% confident.

traps.name: Silent failure
traps.description: Returns an empty result as success, swallows the error or gives a generic message.
traps.principle: Return a structured error (category, retryable, what was attempted, partial results). A failure is not an empty result.
examples: A search subagent that times out returns an empty result list marked as success.
A tool that returns "Operation failed" for every error type.

traps.name: Total failure
traps.description: Ends the whole workflow, or throws, over one recoverable or partial failure.
traps.principle: Recover locally from transient errors, continue with partial results, and pass up only what can't be resolved.
examples: Aborting the whole research report because one of five sources timed out.
Failing the entire batch because three documents out of a thousand were unreadable.

traps.name: Wrong latency mode
traps.description: Uses the Batch API for blocking or interactive work, or a synchronous API for big jobs nothing waits on.
traps.principle: Batch for jobs nothing waits on (overnight, weekly), synchronous for blocking ones (pre-merge, live chat).
examples: Running the pre-merge review check through the Message Batches API to save cost.
Sending 50,000 overnight archive extractions as synchronous calls.

traps.name: Assumed context inheritance
traps.description: Assumes context crosses an agent boundary on its own: a subagent or new session sees the coordinator's history, or the coordinator sees a subagent's intermediate work.
traps.principle: Subagents have isolated context. Pass everything they need explicitly in the prompt; only their final message comes back.
examples: Asking the synthesis subagent to "use the findings above" without including them in its prompt.
Expecting a spawned subagent to know the user's constraints from the coordinator's conversation.
Having the main session read a subagent's intermediate messages, when only its final message comes back.

traps.name: Tool overload
traps.description: Gives one agent many or overlapping tools, or a broad tool outside its role.
traps.principle: Give each agent about 4–5 tools scoped to its role. Use scoped tools for common needs.
examples: Giving the synthesis subagent all 18 tools, including web search, so it searches instead of synthesising.
Giving a document agent a general `fetch_url` tool instead of a `load_document` tool that validates URLs.

traps.name: Same-session self-review
traps.description: Has the same session or instance review its own output.
traps.principle: Use an independent reviewer instance, or a fresh session without the author's reasoning.
examples: Asking the session that generated the code to review it before the PR is opened.
Adding "double-check your answer" to the same extraction call.

traps.name: Aggregate metric masking
traps.description: Trusts an overall accuracy number or average.
traps.principle: Break results down by document type, field and segment before trusting them.
examples: Removing human review because overall extraction accuracy is 97%, while handwritten invoices sit at 70%.
Judging a review bot by its average precision while one category produces most of the false positives.

traps.name: Natural-language termination
traps.description: Ends the loop by parsing assistant text ("done", "complete").
traps.principle: Control the loop with `stop_reason`: continue on `"tool_use"`, stop on `"end_turn"`.
examples: Breaking the agent loop when the assistant's text contains "task complete".
Asking the model to print DONE and checking for that string to stop.

traps.name: Iteration cap as the stopping rule
traps.description: Uses a fixed iteration count as the main way to stop.
traps.principle: Stop on the model's `stop_reason`. A cap is only a safety net, never the main stopping rule.
examples: Running the agent loop exactly 10 times and taking whatever answer exists then.
Raising the iteration limit from 5 to 20 because tasks keep stopping half-done.

traps.name: Nonexistent feature
traps.description: Uses a made-up config key, flag, file or API.
traps.principle: Use the documented mechanism (research §3). Made-up features are always wrong.
examples: Setting a `subagent_inherit_context: true` option that doesn't exist.
Running Claude Code in CI with an invented `--non-interactive` flag instead of `-p`.

traps.name: Escalating too early
traps.description: Hands off to a human or the user when the agent could resolve it (simple issue, transient error, compaction possible).
traps.principle: Resolve what can be resolved. Escalate on explicit criteria only.
examples: Escalating a routine return within policy because the customer sounded frustrated.
Sending a case to a human after a single tool timeout that a retry would fix.

traps.name: Failing to escalate
traps.description: Keeps trying, guesses or decides alone when a human is needed (explicit request, policy gap, no progress, ambiguous identity).
traps.principle: Escalate at once on an explicit human request, a policy exception or no progress. Ask for clarification when something is ambiguous.
examples: Continuing to troubleshoot after the customer has asked twice to speak to a person.
Picking the most recent account when the lookup returns three customers with the same name.

traps.name: Blaming the wrong component
traps.description: Puts the cause of a failure in a component the evidence clears (a subagent that did its assigned part, a step the stem says worked) instead of the one that owns the gap.
traps.principle: Rule out each component the evidence shows working, then look at what owns the gap: the decomposition, the prompt, the handoff or the tool contract.
examples: Blaming a search subagent's narrow queries when it covered the one sector it was given and the coordinator never assigned the rest.
Blaming the synthesis step for a missing topic when it used everything it received.
